questions.question: How is a computational problem formally defined in this lecture?
options: As a function from inputs to a single output.
As a binary relation between inputs and outputs.
As a list of all possible input-output pairs.
As a sequence of steps to reach an output.
questions.answer: As a binary relation between inputs and outputs.
questions.explanation: The lecturer explicitly defines a computational problem as a binary relation between a set of inputs and a set of outputs.
questions.flashcard_front: How is a computational problem formally defined?
questions.flashcard_back: As a binary relation between a set of inputs and a set of outputs.
questions.flashcard_explanation: It is a mapping where edges in a bipartite graph specify which outputs are correct for each input.

questions.question: True or False: A computational problem must map every input to exactly one unique output.
questions.explanation: The lecturer stated that a problem does not necessarily have to map to one output; a single input can map to multiple valid outputs.
questions.flashcard_front: Must a computational problem map an input to exactly one output?
questions.flashcard_back: No, an input can map to multiple valid outputs.
questions.flashcard_explanation: The lecturer used the example of finding an index of a value in an array with multiple occurrences.

questions.question: Why do we typically use predicates to define computational problems instead of listing all input-output pairs?
questions.answer: Listing all pairs is impractical and would take forever for most problems.
questions.explanation: Predicates allow us to check correctness for any input-output pair without needing to enumerate every possible instance of the problem.
questions.flashcard_front: Why use predicates to define problems?
questions.flashcard_back: To verify correctness without listing every possible input-output pair.
questions.flashcard_explanation: Listing pairs is impractical for large or infinite input spaces.

questions.question: In the birthday example, what principle is used to determine that at least two people share a birthday in a large enough group?
questions.explanation: The lecturer cited the pigeonhole principle to explain why, with more than 365 people, a birthday collision is guaranteed.
questions.flashcard_front: What principle guarantees a birthday collision with >365 people?
questions.flashcard_explanation: The lecturer used this to illustrate the power of generalizing problems.
